release.note: The repository's first tag ever. Pre-1.0 deliberately: form1040Report has no production caller, so no server path produces a 1040. The minor position tracks the roadmap phase — 0.11.0 after Phase 11; 1.0.0 reserved for the release in which Phase 14 (Acceptance) lands that path.

most_time_critical.what: Nothing is time-critical. The stakeholder demo happened; the showcase is built, verified and released.
most_time_critical.open_decision: Whether the engine repository and the demo become public — one decision, not two. Needs Sergey.
settled_do_not_relitigate: The demo imports the REAL engine as ES modules. Every fjs/ module is pure; the closure is 43 modules with zero node: imports. Zero dependencies, zero build step.

WASM with a POSIX filesystem is the WRONG answer to the import() question: forbidden dependency, and it undermines the pitch by implying the jail is what makes it safe. The guest never calls import() — it EMITS an import effect.

A demo that runs the real engine in a public page publishes the real engine. The browser must download fjs/** (37 files, ~950 KB, rationale comments included) to execute it. No hosting arrangement avoids this — not a separate public repo, not a vendored snapshot, and a cross-repo read token in a public repo is strictly worse (exfiltratable by any workflow edit, and it does not prevent the disclosure it appears to protect).

Every source/proof link and the build badge point at github.com/fjs-dev/finance, which is PRIVATE. They resolve for org members (a laptop demo is fine) and 404 for everyone else. Repo visibility and demo hosting are therefore one decision.
The demo's links carry the COMMIT, not the tag — a tag can be force-moved and a commit cannot — while the page displays v0.10.0, which is what means something to a reader.
The badge shows the PROJECT-LOCAL proof count only. npm test's total depends on the reader's checkout, so it must never appear on a page.

decisions.rationale: form1040Report has no production caller — no server path produces a Form 1040. A major version would claim what the code cannot do, and it is the exact boundary the demo states out loud on slide one. The minor position tracks the roadmap phase; 1.0.0 is reserved for the release in which Phase 14 lands the end-to-end path.

decisions.decision: The release notes carry 'What is NOT here' at the same volume as what is
decisions.rationale: No production caller, Schedule D selected-then-refusing, four unmodeled document types, guest bodies with host privileges. The demo already tells the truth about these; a release that did not would contradict it in front of the same audience.

decisions.decision: The MCP serverInfo.version is pinned to package.json by the integration test
decisions.rationale: Bumping it to 0.10.0 created the hazard: it is a literal because a pure module has no filesystem to read the manifest from, so it can drift, and a server advertising a version it is not is worse than one advertising none. The test reads the real manifest and compares. Verified load-bearing — set the server to 0.9.9, the test fails with that message.

decisions.decision: npm publish is off the table
decisions.rationale: The name `finance` is already taken on npm by someone else at 0.0.1, and the repository is private. Publishing would need a scoped name such as @fjs-dev/finance, which is a separate decision.

context_notes: Phase 10's lesson was that verification machinery fails silently and in the direction of looking successful. This session produced the environment-and-process twin of it: four of nine commits exist only because something was checked rather than assumed, and in every case the symptom pointed away from the cause. Stale node_modules in two of three checkouts produced sixteen tsc errors INSIDE fjs/** that were not defects in fjs/**, plus a proof count ten short because modules that fail to import never register their proofs. `git add` on the uninitialized submodule silently reverted a staged gitlink, so a commit shipped without the change its own message described — caught only because git ls-tree AFTER the commit is a different check from git diff --cached before it. `git update-index --cacheinfo` accepts a SHA that does not exist. And re-pinning the demo, a path-exists sweep would have passed while an #L anchor pointed at the wrong line, which is worse than a 404 because nothing looks broken. The generalisation, now in AGENTS.md: THE CHECK THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT AND THE CHECK YOU RAN ARE RARELY THE SAME CHECK. Against that, not one wrong number reached a page: every figure in CHANGELOG.md was re-derived from the code while writing it, and the demo recomputes its own regression pair and re-hashes its own printed JSON, shouting on mismatch.
